outcome: The conjecture, previously known only for k ≤ 7 runners, has been extended by a sequence of computer-assisted (non-AI) proofs to k ≤ 13 runners between September 2025 and September 2026; the general conjecture remains open.

disputes.summary: For the k=9 case, Rosenfeld and Trakulthongchai obtained proofs independently within days of each other in November 2025; Trakulthongchai's preprint 'Nine and ten lonely runners' (arXiv:2511.22427) and Rosenfeld's 'The lonely runner conjecture holds for nine runners' (arXiv:2512.01912) both claim k=9, with Trakulthongchai also claiming k=10 in the same paper (later revised, per Sungkawichai & Trakulthongchai 2026, to attribute k=10 to Trakulthongchai alone and extend to k=11,12 jointly). Per the St John's College, Oxford news article, Rosenfeld's work was introduced to Trakulthongchai by Noah Kravitz, and Trakulthongchai's improved sieve method was developed with that starting point in mind, so the two efforts are related rather than fully independent.

summary: Wikipedia's frozen (26 Jan 2024) statement of the lonely runner conjecture — that k runners with pairwise distinct speeds on a unit circular track are all eventually 'lonely' (distance ≥1/k from every other runner) — was, at that date, known only up to k=7 runners (the k=7 case having been settled by Bohman, Holzman & Kleitman-style / Barajas-Serra methods around 2007-2008, well before the window). Starting in September 2025, Matthieu Rosenfeld posted a preprint (arXiv:2509.14111, 'The lonely runner conjecture holds for eight runners') proving the next case, using what the abstract explicitly calls 'a computer verification' combined with recent bounds (from Malikiosis, Santos & Schymura) on the size of a minimal counterexample — i.e. an exhaustive/algorithmic finite check, not a learning-based or generative AI system. Within roughly two months, Rosenfeld (arXiv:2512.01912) and, independently but drawing on Rosenfeld's ideas via an introduction from Noah Kravitz, Oxford undergraduate Tanupat Trakulthongchai (arXiv:2511.22427, 'Nine and ten lonely runners') extended the result to k=9 and (Trakulthongchai alone) k=10, using a refined 'sieve' on top of the same computer-assisted finite-checking framework. In 2026, Touch Sungkawichai and Trakulthongchai further extended the method (arXiv:2604.23906, revised September 2026) to prove k=10, 11, and 12 (the paper's title mentions 13 but the abstract as fetched confirms only up to 12; Quanta and a Wikipedia-adjacent summary suggest 13 may be included in a later revision — this should be checked against the final v2/v3 if precision below 'up to 13' matters). Quanta Magazine's March 2026 piece corroborates the timeline and credits Rosenfeld and Trakulthongchai, describing the methods as 'a computer program, along with ideas from number theory' and 'a more efficient computational technique' — again, classical computer-assisted combinatorial search (SAT-like exhaustive checking / sieving), not AI. I found no evidence anywhere — not in the papers, not in Quanta, not in the Epoch AI 'FrontierMath: Open Problems' page for this conjecture (which merely lists it as an open benchmark problem with no report of an AI attempt), and not in the 'Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search' preprint (which does not mention the lonely runner conjecture at all) — of any AI/ML system being used in these results. A separate August 2026 ScienceDaily story about 'Claude Fable 5' finding a counterexample was, on inspection, about the unrelated Jacobian conjecture, not this problem; I flag this because a naive keyword search could easily conflate the two. Each of these results is a genuine case of the stated conjecture (a restriction to a specific k), so per §3.1 they count as `partial` progress on the problem as stated, correctly matching the triage's routing. The general conjecture (all k) remains open.
competing_reading: One could argue this cluster of results (k=8 through k=12/13) is significant enough progress that a case could be made for 'progress' rather than 'partial' as the primary status label, since no single result resolves a large swath and the trend is a sequence of one-off increments; but per §6.1 'partial' is explicitly defined as 'a case of the problem settled — not a resolution,' which is exactly what each of these is, so I judge 'partial' the correct code rather than 'progress' (which is reserved for a bound moving on a problem that isn't reducible to discrete solved/unsolved cases, or an instructive incident). I record the earliest such event (k=8, Sept 2025) as the decisive `event`, noting the later extensions in this summary rather than fragmenting into multiple records, per the instruction to describe multiple events in `summary`.
what_would_settle_it: Direct confirmation from the final published/revised version of arXiv:2604.23906 (and any successor preprint) on whether k=13 is actually included, and whether any subsequent paper claims k=14 or higher, or whether any lab or researcher has since attempted an AI-driven approach (e.g. an LLM-guided search or a formal-proof-search system) on this specific conjecture.
